title: Back quickly
hook: when events shake you, return to yourself quickly (Meditations 6.11)
carry: give the peg a quick twist

segments.voice: Yesterday: George Long's best revenge, not becoming like the one who wronged you. Your line was not like them. Did a mirrored reply get caught before it left? Day five hundred seventy-five.

A guitarist is halfway through a song when a string slips flat. Everyone hears it. A beginner keeps playing out of tune to the end, mortified. A seasoned player gives the peg a quick twist between phrases and is back in tune before the chorus. Nobody remembers the sour note. They remember the song. Marcus Aurelius uses almost exactly that picture for a shaken mind. The bad news, the slammed door, the sudden scare. The question isn't whether you'll be knocked out of tune. It's how long you stay there.
screen: `A STRING SLIPS FLAT.` → `A QUICK TWIST OF THE PEG.` → `HOW LONG YOU STAY OUT OF TUNE.`

segments.voice: First, the permission. Meditations six, eleven, starts by admitting that circumstances will sometimes force you to be disturbed. Marcus doesn't pretend a Stoic floats above every shock. Things happen that shake anyone. Second, the instruction. In George Long's translation, he tells himself to "quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts." The word quickly matters. Not never wobble. Come back fast. The shock is real for as long as it's happening. Staying shaken after it's over is the part that's optional. Third, the music. The word he uses is harmony, the Greek harmonia, a word for musical tuning and fitting together. He says you'll have more mastery over the harmony by continually returning to it. That's the practice in one sentence. Mastery doesn't come from never slipping. It comes from coming back so often that the way back gets short. A musician who has retuned over and over can do it without stopping the song. Fourth, the everyday version. Modern people have their own words for this. Psychologists talk about recovery time after stress, and some meditation teachers say the moment you notice you've drifted is the moment of practice, not of failure. Those are separate traditions with their own reasons, and none of them is quoting Marcus. But they share his picture. A week ago, in 5.9, Marcus came back after failing. Here the point is speed: how soon you come back after being shaken.
screen: `SHOCKS WILL SHAKE YOU.` · `RETURN TO YOURSELF QUICKLY.` · `MASTERY BY RETURNING OFTEN.` · `THE REP IS COMING BACK.` · then, large: `BACK QUICKLY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find your breath. Just follow it in and out. Before long, your mind may wander, or a sound will startle you, or a worry will pull you off. That's not a mistake. That's the string slipping. When you notice it, give the peg a little twist: come back to the next breath, without scolding. Count how many times you return, if you like. Each return is the whole practice. The bell holds the time.
Back quickly. Marcus's instruction for a shaken mind: you'll be knocked out of tune, so come back fast and often. Today's word.

Your line: give the peg a quick twist. The next time something jolts you today, an email, a near miss, bad news, take one slow breath and say the line. Then return to what you were doing. Day five hundred seventy-five.

howItsDone: Some people who practice meditation or Stoic reflection treat each return from distraction or upset as the exercise itself, aiming to shorten the time they stay shaken rather than to never be shaken.

myth: Marcus says a Stoic should never be disturbed
6.11 admits circumstances will sometimes force you to be disturbed.
Marcus uses a musical picture for returning to yourself
he speaks of being out of tune and of mastering the harmony.
the noticing that you drifted counts as failure
on Marcus's picture, returning often is how mastery is built.

fork.setup: bad news hits mid-morning, and it rattles you hard. by Marcus's line, what now?
options: stay rattled all day so you take it seriously.
feel it, then come back to yourself as soon as the shock has passed.
fork.reveal: Meditations 6.11: return to yourself quickly, and don't stay out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts.

original.note: Greek: a fitting together, a musical tuning; the word in Meditations 6.11.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Stoic should never get rattled.
what it means: you'll be rattled; come back fast, and keep coming back until the way back is short.
what a scholar hears: harmonia first meant a joint or fitting in carpentry and shipbuilding, then a musical tuning; Marcus uses the musical sense.

sources.quoted: quickly return to thyself, and do not continue out of tune longer than the compulsion lasts
